To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the damping provided by a moderately lossy (e.g. stainless steel) manifold is sufficient for the damping of the wakefield and that the emittance growth is reduced by a factor of 2.5 for a 2% lossy manifold.
the wakefield excited by an electron bunch is substantially reduced by plating the manifold walls of a RDDS structure with an electrically conducting, electrically lossy, material.
The damping time of the manifold can be modeled by a single exponential decay with a characteristic time of 2-3 ps for the lossy material canthol, and 5-6 ps for the lossless copper.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of damping structures for the next Linear Collider.
the development of a new class of accelerator structures for use in linear colliders.
the design, fabrication, measurement, and simulation of the wakefield excited by the bunches of electrons in a linear collider.

the damping of the manifold has a very substantial impact on the wakefield, and thus on the BBU and the beam emittance growth.
the damping of the manifold is effective in reducing the wakefield and beam break up, but only for the lowest order modes of the manifold.

The main takeaway from our work is that

, for the case of a lossy manifold, the wakefield can be modeled as a combination of a lossless manifold wakefield, which is driven by a current in the manifold, and a lossy manifold wakefield, driven by the bunch current in the cavity.
the manifold damping must be sufficient to reduce the wakefield by a factor of 10 to 100, depending on the details of the structure and the beam.
the damping of the manifold is very important, and that it can be achieved by using a lossy material or by using stainless steel.
